articles.title: Exclusive: At Starbucks, the future looks smaller
articles.summary: Starbucks is on a mission to recapture its roots as a place to sit down for a cup of coffee. But it doesn’t think it needs a big footprint to deliver on that...
articles.body:
Starbucks is on a mission to recapture its roots as a place to sit down for a cup of coffee. But it doesn't think it needs a big footprint to deliver on that promise.

A new café prototype that opened last month in San Antonio has all the features of a typical Starbucks, like plush seating, bakery treats displayed in a glass case as well as an espresso bar for baristas to make drinks. However, it's a fraction of the size of a usual location.

The new design helps Starbucks push into areas where real estate is expensive, particularly in major cities. Starbucks reworked the counter with a new "folded bar" configuration to fit into narrower spaces rather than running the entirety of a café.

But the chain said the new format still has seating for people to socialize and connect, which has become a hallmark of its reinvigoration plan to recapture the "third place" energy that's a priority for CEO Brian Niccol.

"These particular new formats are really stretching us to be more adaptable to different types of location, different shapes and different sizes, but they still hold all of the aspects of the (coffee house) experience," said Dawn Clark, the company's senior vice president of global concepts and design.

Prior to Niccol's arrival in 2024, Starbucks largely tailored its locations to customers picking up orders off its mobile app. It pulled out 30,000 comfortable seats, installed hard wooden stools and blocked electrical outlets, making cafes a less desirable place to hang out.

Sales suffered as a result, as well as for a variety of other reasons , including higher prices, longer waits for pickup orders and lackluster food options.

In 2025 , as part of a $1 billion restructuring effort, the chain announced a massive renovation plan that brought back cozy seating, more plugs and free refills to encourage customers to stick around. So far, around 1,000 existing locations have been redesigned in North America, with Starbucks planning to accelerate the face lifts.

A smaller-sized prototype could fit into its growth plans.

Starbucks is applying aspects of its broader redesign project to this smaller prototype. It doesn't want repeat the mistakes of the ill-fated pick-up only stores that were created for small spaces.

Niccol shuttered them in July 2025 , saying the locations were "overly transactional." The sterile design didn't have seats and encouraged people to order strictly via its mobile app.

Clark used that as a case study for this design so as to not limit how people order their drinks. About 30% of customers use mobile ordering, the company says.

articles.title: US trade deficit jumped above $100 billion in August
articles.summary: The trade deficit in August was $105.6 billion, a 13.8% increase from July's revised $92.8 billion deficit.
articles.body:
The US trade deficit jumped to more than $100 billion in August as importers wrestled with a new round of President Trump's tariffs and continued to bring in billions of dollars' worth of components for AI data centers.

The total gap: $105.6 billion, a 13.8% increase from July's revised $92.8 billion deficit, the highest level since early 2025, when importers stocked up ahead of Trump's "Liberation Day" and a later four-month surge in imports that pushed average monthly trade deficits north of $120 billion.

Imports rose in August by 4.3%, compared with a 1.4% increase in exports. The US brought in $420.8 billion in total imports in August against $315.2 billion in exports.

In an analysis, Capital Economics said the "sharp rise in imports suggests third quarter GDP growth will be well below our current forecast of 4.0%," suggesting that the final annualized figure could be closer to 2.5%."

"The relatively broad-based rise in goods imports mean net trade was still a drag overall," the group added.

The new data released Tuesday by the Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis showed yet another pivot in global trade, covering the first month after a new phase of Trump's tariffs took effect and the month when trade talks with Canada collapsed .

Demand for artificial intelligence was also evident, with tech companies importing goods to drive the ongoing data center build-out.

The August data showed semiconductor imports increased by $2.4 billion, even as computer accessory imports decreased by $1.6 billion, with overall AI-related imports little changed from July but still elevated.

But a more significant driver of the increase in imports appeared to be industrial supplies. Imports of crude oil jumped by $3.3 billion, and imports of nonmonetary gold increased by $3.1 billion.

It was another surge in goods imports that drove the headline deficit figure, with a goods deficit of $136.57 billion, while the US surplus in service imports stayed essentially flat.

This latest data came after Trump levied new tariffs in late July , including a 10% tariff on top allies like the European Union and a 12.5% tariff on other nations, including China.

The country-by-country breakdown underscored the persistent multibillion-dollar trade deficits that the US runs with a range of countries, from Mexico to Vietnam to the EU.

The largest trade deficit was with Mexico, with a gap of $27.7 billion in August. The deficit with Canada increased by $4.1 billion to $7.1 billion in the month when trade tensions between the US and its northern neighbor escalated.

articles.title: ATF price shock: Govt weighs revival of stabilisation fund as airlines feel fuel heat - report
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The government is weighing a fresh mechanism to stabilise aviation turbine fuel (ATF) prices as the prolonged West Asia crisis pushes up fuel
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The government is weighing a fresh mechanism to stabilise aviation turbine fuel (ATF) prices as the prolonged West Asia crisis pushes up fuel costs and puts increasing pressure on airline finances.A senior government official said the Centre is considering whether to bring back the ATF price stabilisation fund. Specific details of the proposed mechanism were not immediately available, as reported by PTI.Meanwhile, civil aviation minister K Rammohan Naidu said on Tuesday that the government was discussing the issue with airlines and oil marketing companies (OMCs), with ATF prices emerging as a key concern for the industry."One of the most important things is how the West Asia crisis is putting a big burden on ATF prices. We are in discussions with airlines and OMCs (Oil Marketing Companies)," Naidu said on the sidelines of a conference in the national capital.The move comes after the government had introduced a similar support mechanism in June. The Union Cabinet had cleared one-time budgetary support of up to Rs 10,000 crore for OMCs to stabilise ATF prices and support domestic airlines. However, airlines were not keen to use the facility and the scheme has since lapsed.The latest discussions also come as airlines face a sharp increase in fuel costs. ATF accounts for around 40 per cent of an airline's operating expenses, making movements in jet fuel prices a major factor in airline profitability and ticket prices.ATF prices climb, airlines pass on costDomestic ATF prices have risen sharply in recent months. Prices were increased by Rs 5 per litre in August and another Rs 6.28 per litre in September, taking the Delhi rate to Rs 121.28 per litre.On October 1, ATF prices rose by another Rs 16 per litre to around Rs 137 per litre, according to TOI's earlier report, taking the fuel cost to its highest level in years. ICRA estimates that fuel typically accounts for 30-40 per cent of an airline's operating expenses.The impact is already being passed on to passengers.IndiGo, the country's largest airline, announced a hike in fuel charges from October 6 for both domestic and international flights, citing the continuing rise and volatility in ATF prices. The airline said the latest month-on-month increase in fuel prices was more than 14 per cent and had taken ATF costs to among their highest levels in the past decade.The latest move follows an earlier round of ATF-related pressure on airlines. IndiGo had also reduced flight frequencies on some routes in September, with an official citing higher ATF costs linked to the West Asia crisis as one of the factors behind the capacity cuts.The industry, meanwhile, has been pressing the government for a broader overhaul of the way jet fuel is priced.The Federation of Indian Airlines (FIA), which represents Air India, IndiGo and SpiceJet, last month sought a review of the existing ATF pricing formula. It argued that domestic ATF should be priced on the actual cost of fuel plus a reasonable margin instead of being linked to international benchmark pricing.In a letter to the civil aviation ministry, the FIA said the sharp rise in fuel costs, along with geopolitical disruptions and rupee depreciation, was putting significant pressure on airline cash flows and viability.It was earlier reported that airlines were also seeking measures such as a review of the pricing mechanism and relief from taxes and refinery margins as elevated global fuel prices squeezed their margins.ATF prices in India are revised by OMCs on the first day of every month, based on international benchmark prices and foreign exchange rates, with rates also varying across states because of local taxes.You use AI every day. articles.title: Nvidia, Apple, and Microsoft are keeping the stock market afloat
articles.summary: The S&P 500 has never been more concentrated in just three stocks than it is today.
articles.body:
The stock market is pretty much being kept afloat by three tech stocks .

The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) has never been more concentrated in just three stocks than it is today, with Nvidia ( NVDA ), Apple ( AAPL ), and Microsoft ( MSFT ) representing over 21% of the index, per data from Creative Planning.

The importance of these three stocks to the S&P 500 has never been greater. Only IBM ( IBM ), AT&T ( T ), and ExxonMobil ( XOM ) could hold a candle to the three tech stalwarts of today: In the mid-1980s, those three industrial giants at their peak made up 13.4% of the S&P 500.

Nvidia, Apple, and Microsoft have been enjoying higher stock prices over the past month on the back of favorable news, pushing their concentration in the S&P 500 to a record.

The king of AI chips, Nvidia, revealed a stunning new $150 billion stock buyback plan two weeks ago — the largest share repurchase authorization increase in history. It brings the company's total buyback authorization to $235 billion. Shares are now hovering at a record high.

Apple's stock is also trading near a record high. The stock has been on a sizzling run since the company's product unveiling in mid-September.

Apple introduced the iPhone Duo, a device that features a passport-like design that opens and closes like a book. It sports a 5.4-inch front display that expands to a massive 7.6-inch display when opened, ideal for watching movies, playing games, working, and multitasking.

It also unveiled the new iPhone 18 suite and updated AirPods.

Microsoft's stock has also charged ahead, despite arguably lacking the robust recent news flow seen with Nvidia and Apple.

Wall Street analysts have been raising earnings estimates for Microsoft this year and next, citing expectations that AI demand will fuel strong Azure cloud sales.

articles.title: Google signs 20-year nuclear deal with Constellation Energy to power AI build-out
articles.summary: Google has signed a 20-year deal to purchase power from Constellation Energy.
articles.body:
Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ) on Tuesday said it has inked a $4.3 billion deal with Constellation Energy ( CEG ) to bring 890 megawatts of nuclear energy online via a 20-year power purchasing agreement.

Constellation Energy stock climbed more than 12% on the news. Google parent Alphabet stock was flat.

The new capacity, the company said, will come from upgrades at six existing nuclear plants in Illinois, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania, and will include improvements such as modernized turbines, steam generators, and digital control systems.

The tech giant said the agreement provides Constellation with the revenue certainty needed to invest in updates to 11 of its reactors while ensuring customers don't incur additional costs stemming from the AI boom.

As part of the deal, Constellation will use Google's Gemini Enterprise software to help with site selection, outage management, and infrastructure protection.

In addition to the 890-megawatt nuclear plan, Google and Constellation, also agreed to a 15-year energy supply deal for another 2.7 gigawatts of power.

Google has invested in a number of other nuclear projects across the US, including in Georgia, Iowa, and Tennessee, the company said.

Big Tech has been leaning into nuclear energy to meet its power capacity needs amid the AI build-out.

Nuclear power provides clean energy compared with traditional carbon-based power options, though it still carries a significant stigma.

In January, Amazon signed a deal with Constellation for nuclear power, and Microsoft entered a 20-year agreement with the company in 2024, under which it will source energy from one of Constellation's previously shuttered reactors at Three Mile Island by 2028.

Meta ( META ) is also in on nuclear power, signing a 20-year deal to purchase power from Vistra's ( VST ) plants.

Firms are also investing in small modular reactors, compact power plants designed to provide megawatts of power, rather than upwards of 1 gigawatt. A gigawatt is enough energy to power nearly 800,000 homes.

articles.title: He bought a diesel SUV for Rs 13.69 lakh; but repeated DPF issues followed; consumer commission finds deficiency in service and awards Rs 10.99 lakh refund, 9% interest and compensation
articles.summary: Buying a car is a dream, but what if you repeatedly face issues after purchase?
articles.body: Buying a car is a dream, but what if you repeatedly face issues after purchase? In one such case the Kurnool District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has asked the car manufacturer to reimburse an amount to the car buyer along with an interest payment.The Kurnool District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has directed the car manufacturer and its dealer to refund the ex-showroom price of a diesel car to its owner after the vehicle was found to have developed recurring diesel particulate filter (DPF) problems.What the case is aboutA man in Andhra Pradesh, purchased a BS6-compliant Kia Sonet diesel car in 2022. He paid Rs 13.69 lakh for the vehicle. The manufacturer's warranty remained valid until 2025. Ravindranath also opted for an extended warranty, taking the coverage period up to 2027.After some time, the car began developing repeated DPF-related problems. The man consequently took the vehicle to an authorised service centre on several occasions. Various checks, repairs and service interventions were carried out during these visits.These reportedly included examination of the DPF, replacement of a sensor and the battery, removal and refurbishment of the DPF unit and an ECM software upgrade. The service centre eventually removed the DPF and refurbished the unit.The car buyer also incurred an expense of Rs 13,000 for replacing the faulty sensor in his car. He was also advised to replace the battery, although he maintained that the battery was in good condition.Despite these repeated attempts at repair, the problem continued. The car kept developing DPF-related issues over a prolonged period, which the man was able to establish before the consumer commission.The man claimed to have carried out manual DPF regeneration and drove the car under highway conditions as advised, yet the same issue kept recurring.According to the car buyer, the opposite parties were given several chances to rectify the problem but failed to provide a lasting solution for the DPF issue.This remained the case even after extensive repair work, including refurbishment of the DPF and an ECM software upgrade. He claimed that the problem appeared again after the car had travelled only 338 km following these major repairs and the software upgrade.The car manufacturer, however, told the consumer commission that the vehicle had covered more than 43,782 km and had remained roadworthy since it was purchased.“Warranty is subject to its terms and conditions and does not cover issues arising from improper usage, driving patterns, fuel quality, or failure to follow the prescribed operating procedures,” it further said according to an ET report.The manufacturer also disputed the man’s claim that his BS6 diesel SUV was suffering from repeated DPF problems.Its position was that the DPF system fitted in the BS-VI diesel vehicle generates regeneration alerts based on factors such as driving conditions, fuel quality and usage. The manufacturer argued that the mere appearance of such alerts could not, by itself, be taken as proof of a manufacturing defect.The service centre similarly attributed the recurrence of DPF alerts after relatively short driving distances of around 300-500 km to the man’s driving pattern and his alleged failure to follow the prescribed DPF regeneration procedures.Why did the car buyer win the case?The judgment was delivered on September 1, 2026.The consumer commission noted that the vehicle's service history went beyond routine maintenance records. Several job cards specifically documented complaints and work relating to the DPF, including issues involving the DPF sensor and filter, differential pressure sensor, as well as the vehicle's pick-up and performance.The consumer commission said: “The continuity of such entries from 2022 onwards is relevant, particularly when the authorised service centre repeatedly undertook technical interventions in relation to the vehicle.”The commission also considered the manufacturer's argument that the man’s driving pattern was responsible for the recurring DPF problem.It observed that if the owner's driving habits were indeed the main and continuing reason for the issue, the authorised service centre, which had attended to the vehicle on several occasions, should have recorded this conclusion in its service records.The service centre should also have specifically informed the car owner that the recurring problem was linked to the way he was using the vehicle. However, the evidence placed before the consumer commission showed that no such observation or advice was recorded or communicated.The commission also rejected the service centre's suggestion that rat-bite damage was responsible for the recurring DPF problems, finding that this could not account for the repeated issue.It similarly did not accept the argument concerning an ‘abnormal leakage in three fuel injectors’. The commission noted that this issue arose after the DPF problem had already been reported. It could potentially have contributed to the DPF issue, but could not be treated as the sole or complete explanation for the recurring problem.The consumer commission further observed that a diagnosis made at a later stage cannot, by itself, retrospectively override the earlier service history or establish that all the previous complaints had originated from the same cause.The consumer commission made it clear that the mere fact that a vehicle has undergone repeated repairs does not automatically establish a manufacturing defect in the strict technical sense. However, it said the complaint did not necessarily have to be decided solely on whether such a manufacturing defect had been conclusively proved.Instead, the evidence had to be assessed in the context of the warranty obligations and after-sales services provided by the car manufacturer and its authorised service centre.Against this backdrop, the commission found that the repeated attempts to rectify the problem had not succeeded.The consumer commission said: “The opposite parties (car manufacturer Kia and its service centre) have, therefore, failed to provide a satisfactory and durable solution to the recurring defect in the vehicle, amounting to a deficiency in service on their part.”The Kurnool District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission directed Kia and its dealer to pay the car owner Rs 10.99 lakh, which is the ex-showroom price of the vehicle.They were also ordered to pay interest at 9% per annum, Rs 10,000 as compensation for mental agony and another Rs 10,000 towards legal expenses.Malak Bhatt, Chamber Head at Chambers of Malak Bhatt, told ET that the consumer commission's ruling was based on the effectiveness of the after-sales service rather than a finding that the vehicle had a manufacturing defect.The commission specifically acknowledged that repeated repairs, on their own, are not sufficient to establish a manufacturing defect. However, it also held that when the same problem continues to recur despite repeated visits to the service centre, replacement of parts and software upgrades during the warranty period, the consumer has not been given an effective and lasting solution. The commission treated this failure as a deficiency in service.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: El precio medio de la electricidad hoy, miércoles, se sitúa en 182,33 €/MWh, lo que representa una disminución de 19,66 €/MWh en comparación con el día anterior, que cerró en 201,99 €/MWh. Esta caída puede influir en el consumo durante las horas pico, por lo que es relevante identificar las franjas horarias más caras y más baratas para optimizar el gasto en electricidad. Los precios de la luz presentan un marcado aumento durante las primeras horas de la mañana y al final de la tarde; estas franjas horarias son cruciales para entender cuándo resulta más costoso el consumo energético. En particular, se observan picos de precios entre las 07:00 - 08:00 y 08:00 - 09:00, donde alcanzan valores de 237.83 €/MWh y 240.07 €/MWh respectivamente. Además, a última hora del día, entre la 19:00 - 20:00 y 20:00 - 21:00, los precios también se mantienen altos con 227.05 €/MWh y 216.52 €/MWh. Estos datos evidencian que, en total, hay dos bloques de horas concentradas de alta demanda y costo que deben ser considerados por los consumidores. La luz es más barata durante las primeras horas de la mañana y el mediodía, con oportunidades significativas de ahorro. Las franjas horarias más relevantes para beneficiarse de precios bajos se concentran entre las 15:00 - 16:00 con un precio de 86.33 €/MWh, seguida por 14:00 - 15:00 a 109.4 €/MWh y 12:00 - 13:00 a 137.84 €/MWh. En total, hay una ventana amplia entre las 12:00 y 16:00 donde los precios se mantienen por debajo de 140 €/MWh, lo que representa una oportunidad real de ahorro en comparación con las franjas más costosas del día. El análisis de las franjas horarias revela una notable variabilidad en los precios, con una diferencia de hasta 153,61 €/MWh entre la hora más cara y la más barata. Esta amplia amplitud en los precios puede resultar relevante para los consumidores, ya que les brinda la oportunidad de programar su consumo en los momentos más económicos, optimizando así su factura eléctrica.

articles.title: The Emmys are leaving broadcast TV for Amazon’s Prime Video
articles.summary: The Emmy Awards are headed to Amazon Prime Video, ending the ceremony’s decades-long rotation among the broadcast television networks.
articles.body: The Emmy Awards are headed to Amazon Prime Video, ending the ceremony’s decades-long rotation among the broadcast television networks. Under a six-year deal announced Tuesday morning, the Emmys will exclusively stream on Prime Video beginning in September 2027. Viewers will be able to watch for free, without a subscription. The agreement replaces the arrangement under which ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC took turns airing television’s biggest awards show. It follows last year’s announcement that the Oscars will leave ABC for YouTube beginning in 2029. “Television has never been more global, and the Emmys should be a celebration that the world can share,” Cris Abrego, chair of the Television Academy, said in a statement. “Now Prime Video audiences in more than 200 countries will be able to experience the Emmys live with no subscription required.” The move ends a broadcast network run stretching back to 1955, when NBC first aired the Emmys nationally. NBC also carried this year’s ceremony, the last under the rotating agreement. Final audience numbers for the 2026 Emmys showed 6.8 million viewers, down 10% from the previous year. Amazon and the Television Academy said the partnership would include new ways for fans to engage with the show throughout the year, though they did not detail those plans. The agreement gives Prime Video another marquee live event as streaming platforms compete for viewers. In addition to the YouTube Oscars deal, Disney will begin carrying the Grammy Awards across ABC, Hulu and Disney+ starting next year.

articles.title: Forget Buc-ee’s, this is the US’s favorite convenience store, new report shows
articles.summary: Depending on where you live, you may not have even been aware that this brand offers gas.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – If you had to guess America’s favorite convenience store, the first brand that comes to mind may be Buc-ee’s, especially based on its fandom and regardless of whether you’ve been to one yourself.

You would be wrong, according to a new report.

The latest data from the American Customer Satisfaction Index (ACSI) shows that an entirely different retailer, known primarily for serving an entirely different industry, is the top convenience store brand in the U.S.

More than two dozen brands were considered this year by the ACSI, and then ranked based on their scores across surveyed customers. Benchmarks analyzed included store hours and locations, food quality, store layout and cleanliness, merchandise variety, and even the quality and freshness of coffee.

Topping the list last year was Kwik Trip, the Wisconsin-based fuel chain that has spread throughout the Midwest. The brand slipped slightly this year, ranking third overall on ACSI’s rankings.

Plowing to the top is another Midwest-based brand: Meijer.

You may better recognize the name for the hundreds of grocery stores it operates across six states: its home state of Michigan, as well as Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Wisconsin, and Kentucky. Many of those locations also offer fueling stations, which scored the highest customer satisfaction rates among those surveyed this year.

Meijer improved five points to a score of 82 out of 100 on this year’s report. The ACSI noted that customers appreciate the retailer’s rewards program, which reportedly saved customers $200 million over the previous year.

Meijer did not, however, rank as the top-rated brand in the Midwest, according to the ACSI. That spot was claimed by Sheetz, which edged out Meijer by a single point when broken down by region.

Wawa was the top spot in the Northeast and the South. In the latter, Wawa edged out Buc-ee’s by a single point. In the West, Maverik and QuikTrip tied.

You can view the top convenience store chains and their scores (out of 100), according to ACSI’s customer satisfaction rankings below, and its full study here .

Buc-ee’s, Maverik, Pilot, RaceTrac, and Shell: 77

No convenience store chain fell as much in the rankings as Kwik Trip, which lost six points off last year’s score, ACSI’s data shows. Three chains — Love’s, Cumberland Farms, and Sunoco — dropped five points.

articles.title: Karnataka Beer Sales Surge 41% as New Alcohol Tax Boosts Revenue
articles.summary: Karnataka beer sales rose 41.3% in Apr–Sep as new alcohol-by-content tax lifted liquor revenue 13.4% to Rs 22,191 crore; IMFL sales up 1.1%.
articles.body: Bengaluru: Beer sales in Karnataka rose 41.3% year-on-year during April-September, reversing a 19% decline in the corresponding period last year, according to govt figures cited by the Brewers Association of India (BAI).The state’s liquor tax collections increased 13.4% to Rs 22,191 crore during the six months. Collections had grown 2.8% in the same period last year, the industry body said.The sharp recovery in beer contrasted with slower growth in spirits. Sales of Indian-made foreign liquor (IMFL), which includes whisky, rum and vodka, increased 1.1%. Tax collections from the category rose 13%, while those from beer increased 19%.BAI linked the performance to Karnataka’s alcohol-in-beverage taxation framework, introduced on May 11. The system levies excise duty on the actual quantity of alcohol in a beverage. An additional excise duty is linked to the product’s value.“Several other states are keenly watching its implementation in Karnataka and we hope that these results will encourage more States to follow suit,” said Vinod Giri, director general of BAI.The association said the growth in IMFL sales and tax receipts eased concerns that the new framework would hurt the spirits industry. It also suggested that consumers could be moving towards more expensive liquor products.Giri argued that the framework encouraged consumers to choose beverages with lower alcohol content while supporting govt revenues. However, the sales and tax figures cited in the release do not establish whether overall alcohol consumption or alcohol-related harm declined.BAI represents beer makers including AB InBev, Carlsberg and United Breweries.You use AI every day. articles.title: Support for small businesses suggests socialism’s shine is overstated
articles.summary: In an op-ed, Elaine Parker argues that rising costs in healthcare, childcare, and housing stem from government regulation and deficit spending rather than capitalism, suggesting that increased free-market principles could alleviate both inflation and growing support for socialism.
articles.body:
A new Gallup poll finds a record number of Americans support socialism, with 43 percent of respondents viewing it favorably.

Judging by the dozens of breathless headlines , this seems like a significant and concerning ideological shift, especially alongside declining post-pandemic support for capitalism.

But on closer reflection, respondents are likely just fed up with the economic status quo, falsely labeled capitalism, rather than actually wanting more government control over their economic lives.

Ordinary Americans are facing a persistent affordability crisis driven mostly by the costs of healthcare, childcare, housing, and overall inflation. Ironically, these major financial hurdles result from big government and socialist policies, not capitalism.

Consider healthcare, which some polls suggest is Americans’ most significant economic concern. Per capita health expenditures have more than tripled this century. Four-figure monthly insurance premiums and five-figure hospital bills have generated a mass movement to socialize the system under a Medicare for All approach.

Yet the current system doesn’t resemble anything close to capitalism. In fact, big-government regulations that have essentially banned catastrophic insurance, association health plans, and other competing coverage alternatives are responsible for sky-high premiums. Certificate-of-need laws, bans on physicians owning hospitals, and burdensome medical licensing requirements prevent new provider competition.

As a result, hospitals and health insurers have consolidated into expensive oligopolies that can have terrible customer service, hide their prices, and overcharge for basic care and coverage. Such practices would never occur in a free market.

It’s a similar story for childcare, whose escalating costs have led some left-of-center politicians, such as Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) , to call for socialization. This is also true of housing, whose prices have increased by 60 percent since the beginning of 2020.

However, childcare and housing costs are inflated by countless burdensome state and local regulations that prevent new supply. In childcare, stringent regulations on caregiver ratios, occupational licensing, and square footage lock out competitors. In housing, strict zoning, rent control, eviction, environmental, and labor laws reduce housing stock and drive up costs.

Finally, there’s the runaway prices of general goods and services, which have inflated faster than average wages for most of this decade. Every time an American pays $18 for a burrito, $100 for a few groceries, or $250 to service their vehicle, they are reminded that the economic status quo isn’t working.

Yet rising costs aren’t the result of greedy capitalists. In fact, businesses constantly look for ways to lower prices to attract more customers and increase profits. The prolonged high inflation crushing ordinary families stems from reckless government deficit spending that increases interest rates and the money supply.

Recent federal deficits have approached $2 trillion annually , contributing to the current bond market turmoil that’s boosting borrowing costs and threatening the broader economy and financial system.

To monetize these deficits, the money supply has increased by 50 percent since 2020. More money dilutes the currency already in existence. In the words of Milton Friedman, “Inflation is everywhere and anywhere a monetary phenomenon.”

Expensive socialist programs to address the affordability crisis would only make inflation worse. Existing reckless social spending must end to finally whip inflation.

An honest media, a good education system, and integral politicians are desperately needed to explain these economic nuances. Unfortunately, they demagogue and simplify the issues to advance their partisan and ideological goals. The Democratic Socialists of America have stepped into this vacuum with claims that socialism is the savior — not the culprit — of today’s economic pain.

Nonprofit free-market organizations have never been more needed to educate the public about how socialism takes and capitalism creates.

The Gallup poll includes another finding that suggests support for socialism is overstated: It finds an incredible 95 percent of Americans support small businesses.

Small businesses are the embodiment of capitalism in today’s economy. They are characterized by entrepreneurship, investment, private ownership, competition, and voluntary exchange. They are also on the front lines of the economy and are the hardest hit by socialist policies such as high taxes, burdensome regulations and runaway inflation.

True supporters of small businesses can’t also support socialism — at least in practice.

To preserve America’s wildly popular small business economy, we need more capitalism and less socialism. The effects of such a transformation will be twofold: much-improved economic well-being for ordinary Americans and significantly reduced popular support for socialism.

Elaine Parker is president of Job Creators Network Foundation.

articles.body: US stocks moved closer to record highs on Tuesday, helped by stronger earnings expectations, easing oil prices and a renewed rally in technology shares.The S&P 500 rose 0.8 per cent and was on course to close above its previous record set in August. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 343 points, or 0.7 per cent, while the Nasdaq Composite added 0.8%, moving towards a fresh record after reaching an all-time high a day earlier.The gains have come despite continued concerns over inflation, elevated bond yields and the economic impact of the war with Iran. The S&P 500 has risen nearly 24% since hitting its low in late March.A key support for the rally has been expectations of stronger corporate profits. Analysts expect companies in the S&P 500 to report nearly 30% growth in earnings per share for the July-September quarter, according to FactSet. If realised, it would mark the third consecutive quarter in which earnings growth exceeded 25%.The easing in oil prices also provided some relief. Brent crude fell 1.1% to $99.19 a barrel, down from nearly $110 a few weeks ago. The decline helped push the yield on the 10-year US Treasury note down to 5.26%, from 5.31% on Monday.Software stocks stage a comebackUS software stocks have emerged as another driver of the market's recent strength, with investors increasingly betting that artificial intelligence will help rather than destroy demand for many software companies.The S&P 500 software and services index rose 1.3 per cent on Tuesday to its highest level since November 2025. The index also recorded its strongest quarterly gain since the second quarter of 2020 during the July-September period.Companies including Salesforce, ServiceNow and Accenture have reported strong results, while partnerships with AI companies have helped improve sentiment towards the sector. Cybersecurity stocks have performed particularly strongly as businesses increase spending to protect systems in the age of AI.CrowdStrike, Fortinet and Palo Alto Networks have all recorded triple-digit gains this year.“AI has been more of an enabler for a lot of these software companies, more than a disruptor,” said Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist at LPL Financial.The software index is up about 5% this year, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index has surged 87.5%, although chip stocks have pulled back from their highs. Meanwhile, expectations for software-sector earnings growth in 2026 have climbed to 20.6%, from 13.8% at the end of March, according to LSEG data.Software stocks suffered a sharp selloff earlier this year, with the sector falling more than 26% from late January to its April low. The decline was driven by fears that companies could use AI to develop software internally at a much lower cost, threatening traditional software providers.Those concerns now appear to have eased as companies report continued demand and greater adoption of AI tools.“The whole SaaSpocalypse didn't happen anywhere near as fast as some of the people on Wall Street thought it would,” said Rebecca Wettemann, CEO of technology research firm Valoir.However, analysts warn that AI remains a longer-term risk for the industry. Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management, said the more significant test for software companies could come in the second half of 2027, when greater data-centre capacity could make AI-powered coding a bigger challenge for traditional software businesses.Additionallly, several major companies are due to report results in the coming days. articles.title: Judge skeptical of FCC’s move to scrutinize ABC station licenses
articles.summary: A federal judge in D.C. on Tuesday declined to immediately rule on whether the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) should be stopped from conducting an early review of broadcast licenses belonging to a handful of local ABC stations across the country. articles.body:
A federal judge in D.C. on Tuesday declined to immediately rule on whether the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) should be stopped from conducting an early review of broadcast licenses belonging to a handful of local ABC stations across the country.

But U.S. District Judge Loren Alikhan appeared skeptical from the bench of the administration’s justification for initiating the process.

“What is it that made this so different that you needed to call for an early license renewal?” Alikhan asked a Justice Department lawyer during Tuesday’s two-hour hearing, getting to the heart of the administration’s efforts to scrutinize the Disney-owned broadcaster.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The Trump administration contends that the FCC’s early renewal process, an unprecedented move for a media regulator to take against one of the nation’s largest broadcast networks, was necessary as part of the department’s probe into Disney’s diversity, equity and inclusion hiring practices.

“The commission has an obligation to pursue these types of investigations,” Dimitar Georgiev, an attorney for the DOJ, said, framing it as a “core function” of the Brendan Carr-led agency.

ABC sued the FCC in August, accusing the Trump administration of embarking on a “retaliatory campaign” to punish the network for unfavorable coverage and commentary about the Trump administration.

The sprawling media company that encompasses ABC News, ESPN and a massive movie studio is seeking a preliminary injunction that would block the early renewal process from moving forward.

“There’s no doubt that this conduct is unconstitutional,” ABC attorney Beth Wilkinson said, likening possible license revocation to what she called the “corporate death penalty.”

Wilkinson argued on-air employees at ABC on popular shows like “The View” have been “chilled” by the FCC’s move to scrutinize the network’s broadcast licenses and caused the company immediate and irreparable harm that is impacting its coverage of the coming midterm elections.

“Our editorial decisions are being affected right now before the election,” she said, later citing ABC’s decision to pull a late-night interview with Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico off the air and put it on YouTube instead.

DOJ lawyers attempted to convince the judge that ABC’s lawsuit should be dismissed, arguing the district court does not have jurisdiction over the case.

Georgiev pointed to a provision in the Communications Act that gives the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals authority to review license applications that are denied by the FCC, arguing that halting the process would “sidestep” Congress.

But Wilkinson contended that would leave Disney with no recourse to pursue its First Amendment retaliation claims if the licenses are not revoked.

“Our concern is we are chilled,” Wilkinson added. “That kind of immediate harm cannot be rectified by the Court of Appeals.”

The Trump administration has also accused Disney of flouting its obligations that come with accessing public airwaves.

Tuesday’s court proceeding was the latest episode in months of tensions between President Trump’s FCC and the Disney-owned broadcast network.

Carr, an ally of Trump, has cast doubt on the agency’s independence and defended the president’s attacks on mainstream media outlets.

He has repeatedly criticized ABC over its news coverage and called for the firing of the network’s top comedian, Jimmy Kimmel, over jokes he made about the Republican response to the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk.

During his time as FCC chair, Carr has questioned whether late-night and daytime talk programs like Kimmel’s and ABC’s “The View” are so-called “bona fide” news programs and should be able to use public airwaves.

Licenses for the local stations — in major markets like New York, Los Angeles and Houston — were not scheduled to be up for renewal until between 2028 and 2031.

ABC described that inquiry as “pretextual” and rejected the administration’s claim that it has not fully cooperated with demands for information.

The judge did not issue a ruling from the bench, instead asking the Trump administration to answer in writing what other mechanisms it could use to compel ABC’s cooperation with its probe.

articles.title: Noem refutes report her DHS bought planes at inflated prices from donor
articles.summary: The five planes were purchased the morning before Noem left her role.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — The Department of Homeland Security reportedly bought five planes at inflated prices from a political donor to then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem just hours before she left office — a charge she refutes.

The agency purchased the planes from Daedalus Aviation Corporation and paid $108 million for a Boeing 737 converted to a private jet, $106 million for a pair of Gulfstream jets and $45 million each for two Boeing 737 passenger jets, according to reporting by The New York Times .

The paper reported that the planes were purchased the morning before Noem left office. She had been fired on March 5 following several controversies but remained in the role until Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin took over on March 24.

In a post on social platform X , Noem pushed back, calling the paper “dishonest” and saying that “numerous corrections” had been made. She also called the term donor “misleading.”

William Walters, the head of Daedalus, donated $10,000 to political action committee American Resolve, which supported Noem. The planes were reportedly purchased at a large markup from what Daedalus originally paid to acquire them.

“If the individual did not personally make political contributions to Secretary Noem, or if the term ‘donor’ instead refers indirectly to unrelated entities or legally distinct contributions, the article simply fails to meet the standards of precision expected of The New York Times,” the former secretary wrote.

The $108 million Boeing 737 private plane was reportedly bought by Daedalus for less than $90 million a few months before DHS purchased it, according to the report. The Gulfstreams that Daedalus sold for $106 million were reportedly purchased for $83 million, said to be millions more than market prices.

The five planes make up half of a 10-plane purchase the Times previously reported on, which DHS said was necessary for deportation flights . However, without crews to fly them, the planes have gone largely unused.

In addition to the no-bid contract with Daedalus to purchase planes, the agency also hired Salus Worldwide, another company owned by Walters, to care for the purchased planes. That same company was also hired by DHS to fly Noem and her aides on chartered planes and to encourage immigrants to self-deport .

NewsNation reached out to DHS for comment.

articles.title: ‘System already straining’: Global oil buffers shrink amid mounting supply risks, say industry leaders
articles.summary: The global oil market is entering the winter with a much thinner safety cushion after more than 1 billion barrels were taken out of commercial stockpiles
articles.body: The global oil market is entering the winter with a much thinner safety cushion after more than 1 billion barrels were taken out of commercial stockpiles during this year's supply disruptions, industry executives said at a London energy conference.The concern is not simply how much oil is sitting in storage, but how much of it can actually reach the market. Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser said less than 6 billion barrels of commercial inventories remain globally, with only 10% or less considered practically available.“Less than 6 billion barrels of commercial inventories remain today, with the vast majority not practically available, so the system is already straining,” Nasser said at the Energy Intelligence Forum, as quoted by Reuters.Oil can be counted as inventory without being immediately usable. Some crude is effectively tied up in pipelines or tank bottoms, while governments keep emergency reserves that cannot routinely be tapped. This leaves a much smaller pool of barrels that traders can access when supply suddenly falls.That is becoming a bigger concern as global oil consumption is running at about 102 million barrels a day, according to the International Energy Agency. With fewer readily available barrels in storage, another major disruption could have a larger impact on prices.Why inventories have been drainedGovernments and energy companies have been relying on stored oil to compensate for supply disruptions linked to the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine. More than 1 billion barrels have been released, mainly from commercial inventories, since the latest Middle East crisis began, Nasser said.The drawdown has effectively used up much of the buffer that normally helps the market absorb temporary supply shocks. Rebuilding those stocks could take years because producers would have to add oil to storage while continuing to meet everyday global demand.Chevron CEO Mike Wirth said the loss of these buffers had made the oil market more fragile and increased the price floor for crude.The reduced cushion also leaves the market increasingly dependent on supplies that are still flowing, particularly seaborne exports from the Middle East. Vitol CEO Russell Hardy said there were few additional inventories left in Western markets that could be drained to make up for a fresh shortfall.The US is also entering the period with a much smaller emergency crude cushion. Stocks in the country's Strategic Petroleum Reserve have fallen to their lowest level since October 1982, according to Department of Energy data.The reserve is designed to provide additional crude during major supply disruptions, meaning its depletedIEA plans 100 million-barrel releaseThe IEA is preparing to release 100 million barrels of crude and diesel as it seeks to ease pressure in the market, particularly on diesel prices.Nasser said the decision followed negotiations over how much oil could realistically be made available. It is not yet clear how much of the planned release will consist of barrels from the IEA's record 400 million-barrel release in March that had not yet reached the market.The fresh release highlights the limited availability of emergency supplies. “Inventories are reaching a stress level. Only 10% or less is available,” Nasser said.The intervention could provide some near-term relief, but executives at the London forum warned that replenishing depleted inventories would remain a challenge.You use AI every day. President Trump will give remarks Tuesday afternoon in Baltimore to unveil a multibillion-dollar investment aimed at boosting U.S. submarine production.

Defense technology company Anduril Industries plans to invest $3.7 billion in a new shipyard at Tradepoint Atlantic in Sparrows Point, while the Navy could spend up to another $2.9 billion purchasing production from the facility.

The shipyard, dubbed Arsenal-2, will manufacture components and large-scale assemblies for the Pentagon’s Virginia-class attack submarines. The project is expected to create more than 3,000 permanent jobs.

articles.title: Adani airports stop processing export cargo to Russia, 150 tonnes delayed
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Adani Airport Holdings Ltd (AAHL), which operates eight airports including Mumbai, Navi Mumbai and Ahmedabad, has stopped processing export cargo
articles.body: MUMBAI: Adani Airport Holdings Ltd (AAHL), which operates eight airports including Mumbai, Navi Mumbai and Ahmedabad, has stopped processing export cargo bound for Russia, leaving about 150 tonnes backlog of air cargo, primarily pharmaceuticals, machinery and spare parts, awaiting clearance for the past 10 days.“Among the cargo held up are government-to-government supplies that move regularly on this route under the special and privileged strategic partnership reaffirmed at the highest level by India and Russia,” said a source.The affected shipments are those booked on Russian national carrier Aeroflot, which flies daily from Delhi and five times a week from Goa, as well as non-scheduled Russian Freighter carrier Volga-Dnepr. Aeroflot doesn’t operate scheduled flights to/from Mumbai or any other AAHL-managed airport. But cargo from Mumbai and other parts of western and southern India bound for Russia are routed via Mumbai because of availability of export registration facilities.At Mumbai the cargo undergoes export processing: cargo is brought by road and is granted entry into the airport cargo complex, where it is accepted, security-screened and cleared by customs. Thereafter, the cargo is flown to Delhi or Goa on domestic carriers such as IndiGo or Blue Dart, or transported by road via bonded trucks to these airports for loading onto the Russian flights.Shubham Singh, director, SW Trading, the official cargo sales agent for Aeroflot, pan India said: "Aeroflot is the only national carrier flying directly from India to Moscow daily. If this is not resolved soon, cargo moving from Mumbai will face serious disruption and the India-Russia trade lane will be affected."On Sept 23, SW Trading wrote to Mumbai International Airport Ltd (MIAL), saying its trucks had been “waiting for carting orders for the last 3-4 days but no response”. “We are paying heavy storage charges and truck detention charges therefore kindly consider our request on priority and assist,” the letter said.With no response from the airport operator, the company sought government intervention, writing to the ministries of civil aviation, external affairs, commissioner of customs and home affairs, among others. Sources said the government has begun looking into the matter and an intervention is expected soon. “When we asked why they had stopped processing exports to Russia, the officials at the Mumbai airport told us that they had orders from their headquarters,” said a source, adding that about 104 Indian companies supply medicines to Russia.The curb came days after the Adani group raised $1 billion from funds managed by US-based BlackRock. An Economic Times report said the decision was linked to sanctions imposed on Russia by the US Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC).In its letter, SW Trading contended that AAHL, having been appointed custodian under the Customs Act by the government, was mandated to provide cargo services to airlines without discrimination. “Refusal to handle cargo of a specific country or airline, especially a scheduled carrier is contrary to your custodial obligations,” the letter said.The cargo agent has also asked Customs to direct the airport to state in writing the specific grounds for refusing or preventing the processing of cargo booked on Aeroflot, including the precise instruction, order or document on which the decision was based. Delmos Aviation Pvt Ltd, general sales and service agent for Aeroflot too has taken up the matter with the government.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: The Emmy Awards is going streaming — after more than 75 years on broadcast TV, the ceremony is making the move to Amazon Prime Video. The Television Academy, which holds the annual awards gala, and Prime Video announced Tuesday that they inked a “historic, multiyear deal” that will make the streaming giant the new home…
articles.body:
The Emmy Awards is going streaming — after more than 75 years on broadcast TV, the ceremony is making the move to Amazon Prime Video.

The Television Academy, which holds the annual awards gala, and Prime Video announced Tuesday that they inked a “historic, multiyear deal” that will make the streaming giant the new home for the ceremony.

As part of a six-year deal, Prime Video will become “the exclusive global home of the Emmy Awards, ushering in a bold, innovative vision to propel the cultural icon into its next chapter,” an announcement said.

Since 1949, when it was launched, the Emmys has aired on a rotating basis among the major broadcast networks. The switch to Prime Video will begin with the September 2027 awards ceremony.

Prime Video and the Television Academy said that next year’s ceremony won’t be behind a paywall and “will be free to view for audiences worldwide.”

The awards show is the latest event to jump from broadcast TV to a streaming platform. In 2021, the NFL announced it had reached a deal to make Prime Video its exclusive partner for Thursday Night Football. The move marked the first time a streaming service had a full game package.

The Television Academy and Prime Video touted the agreement, which they said will transform the Emmys “into a year-round cultural celebration” that will deliver “new experiences and entry points for fans to discover, engage with and celebrate what they love about TV.”

articles.title: David Ellison backs CNN’s Trump lawsuit, pledges editorial independence
articles.summary: CNN’s new owner, David Ellison, says he supports CNN’s legal action against the Trump administration over White House access, and will not interfere in the news organization’s coverage.
articles.body: CNN’s new owner, David Ellison, says he supports CNN’s legal action against the Trump administration over White House access, and will not interfere in the news organization’s coverage. “We believe in editorial independence, and we will never interfere,” Ellison said, reiterating the reassurances he made while seeking to buy Warner Bros. Discovery earlier this year. The merger between Warner and Paramount took effect on Tuesday morning, and Ellison held an employee town hall to introduce the newly combined company, named Skydance. Ellison, the CEO of Skydance, laid out his vision for investing in films, shows and new technology. “For the first time,” he said, “we have the studios, the franchises, the libraries, the talent and scale all under one roof to compete with anyone in the world.” CNN anchor Anderson Cooper interviewed Ellison at the town hall and asked directly about CNN employees’ concerns about Skydance’s ownership. In response, Ellison said, “I believe deeply in journalism,” and went on to call the work done by CBS News and CNN “a vital part of our democracy.” While speaking about the need for fact-based news, Ellison said, “You go back to what President Obama said during the pandemic. He said a republic that can’t agree on the same set of facts can’t function, and I think he was 100% right about that.” In the news space, “we want to actually help scale and transition the business digitally,” Ellison said. He emphasized the importance of growing CNN’s digital operations and reaching new audiences worldwide, citing Skydance’s estimate that the combined company reaches more than 200 million streaming subscribers. The newly formed company, he said, “can create an even bigger platform for the best journalism in the world.” The Ellison family’s ties to President Donald Trump had fueled concerns among CNN employees about the network’s independence. Last fall, Trump described Ellison and his father, the billionaire Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, as “friends of mine” and “big supporters of mine.” Last December, Trump said “it’s imperative that CNN be sold” to new owners. Asked about the merger by a reporter on Tuesday afternoon, Trump said, “It’s going to be a great company. They’re terrific people, and it’s going to be a great company.” At the Skydance town hall, Cooper asked a follow-up question about CNN, MS NOW and Politico’s First Amendment lawsuit over Trump’s recent attempt to ban the three news outlets from the White House. Cooper asked, “Do you stand with CNN and our effort to completely restore access to covering President Trump?” “Of course,” Ellison said. The next hearing in the legal case is slated for Thursday morning. Both CNN chairman and editor-in-chief Mark Thompson and CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss attended the town hall. The two news operations are operating separately for now. “We trust Mark, we trust the team,” Ellison said while speaking about CNN. Later on, Cooper asked about the likelihood of a tie-up between CBS and CNN in the future: “If Paramount and Warner Brothers are now cousins, and CBS News and CNN are cousins, when does somebody start to ask them to share organs?” “It’s day one,” Ellison said. He said he intends to bring the relevant business leaders “into the decision-making” now that the deal has taken effect. Generally speaking, companies will start making integration decisions “within usually 120 days,” Ellison said, “but I think it’s foolish to try to say I’m going to show up with every single answer today.”

articles.title: Why Flavio Bolsonaro outperformed the polls in Brazil’s election
articles.summary: A late right-wing shift, a banking scandal and economic frustration may be behind Bolsonaro’s last-minute gains.
articles.body:
With three weeks to go until Brazil’s presidential runoff, President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva finds himself in a weaker position than he — or most pollsters — had expected.

A second round of voting was widely predicted. But most recent polls had Lula entering a runoff from first place, putting him about three percentage points ahead of rival Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.

Instead, Bolsonaro took about 47 percent of the vote on Sunday to Lula’s 45 percent, a reversal that surprised analysts and raised questions about what happened in the final days of the campaign, and what the polls may have missed.

Carlos Pereira, a political scientist at the Getulio Vargas Foundation think-tank in Brazil, believes part of the answer lies in a late shift among voters who had planned to support smaller right-wing candidates.

Bolsonaro himself had said he was banking on exactly that, telling reporters on election day that he expected a “protest vote” from people who might have otherwise backed another candidate but were united in their opposition to Lula.

“Usually, voters, they vote [sincerely] in the first round, and they vote strategically in the second round,” Pereira told Al Jazeera.

This time, he said, some voters who were planning to cast their ballot for candidates like the former governor of the central state of Goias, Ronaldo Caiado, and businessman and founder of the right-wing Free Brazil Movement, Renan Santos, appear to have made the strategic choice earlier.

“They thought, ‘Let’s try to resolve this election right now,’” Pereira said. “If you’re gonna vote for Flavio anyway in the second round, why not vote for him right now?”

That early consolidation could also matter in the runoff. Political analyst Rafael Favetti told Reuters news agency that some of the support Bolsonaro would have usually picked up only in a second round had already been “front-loaded,” potentially leaving him less room to expand his coalition.

Another factor, Pereira said, was the Banco Master scandal , a sprawling alleged banking fraud that rattled both campaigns in the final weeks, touching figures across the political spectrum.

Among them was Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw the case that sent Bolsonaro’s father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, to prison. De Moraes was accused of improper ties to Banco Master owner Daniel Vorcaro after documents emerged appearing to show the banker seeking legal advice from him. De Moraes has denied the allegations.

Pereira believes that connection may have acted as a late “trigger” for some voters. Bolsonaro’s supporters have seen Moraes as a political ally of Lula, with Flavio making a direct link between the two on the campaign trail earlier this year, saying, “Anyone voting for Lula is voting for Alexandre de Moraes.”

A September Datafolha poll found 34 percent of Brazilians associated the Banco Master scandal more with the left, compared with 27 percent who associated it more with the right.

Andre Pagliarini, a professor of history and international studies at Louisiana State University and author of Lula: A People’s President and the Fight for Brazil’s Future, agreed the scandal may have hurt the president. A campaign dominated by “spectacular, unceasing scandal involving seemingly the entire political class”, he said, played to Bolsonaro’s strengths as an “anti-institutional insurgent”.

“The irony, of course, is that Flavio himself was directly implicated in the Banco Master scandal in a way that Lula is not,” he said in an email.

The younger Bolsonaro is under investigation over allegations that he sought money from Vorcaro to finance a film about his father. He denies wrongdoing.

Neither analyst saw the result as a wholesale failure of the polls.

For Pagliarini, the bigger surprise was the scale of support for the right, which extended well beyond the presidential race.

Bolsonaro won nearly four percentage points more than his father did in the first round in 2022, while his Liberal Party emerged with the largest bloc in Brazil’s Senate. The right also came out strong in gubernatorial races and made significant gains in the southeast of the country.

“There clearly was a powerful information environment around Flavio that allowed his campaign to keep its message in front of voters even as the mainstream press exposed scandal after scandal,” said Pagliarini. “If anything, the polls underestimated the commitment of voters already leaning right.”

But the results also point to a deeper challenge for Lula and the Brazilian left: a sense among many voters that the government is not delivering enough, particularly on the economy and public security.

On paper, Lula can point to a number of positive economic indicators, like record-low unemployment, falling inequality and easing inflation. But that hasn’t necessarily translated into a sense that life is getting easier, as Brazilians have continued to feel squeezed by high food prices and household debt.

A September Quaest poll found nearly half of those surveyed believed the economy had gotten worse over the previous year, compared with just 19 percent who thought it had improved.

“Voters can acknowledge that poverty is down and unemployment is low and still feel overworked, indebted, unsafe and fed up with political conflict,” Pagliarini said. “The right has figured out how to turn those frustrations into a very clear political identity.”

Lula now has three weeks to close a gap of about 2.2 million votes. And there are millions potentially up for grabs.

About nine million votes went to other candidates in the first round, while more than 33.4 million Brazilians didn’t vote – 28 percent of registered voters.

“It’s possible, but the arithmetic is tough,” Pagliarini said.

For Lula to turn things around, he’d need to win voters who backed minor candidates, reach some of those who abstained and find more support in the northeast, which is already his strongest region.

His campaign is preparing a new communications team. Pargliarini said he’ll be watching the debates, where Lula could make a case directly against Bolsonaro rather than against his brand.

“The odds are steep, but Lula remains an extremely powerful communicator,” he said. “Going hard at Flavio in this round is his only hope.”

articles.title: ABC to federal judge: Trump’s FCC is holding our head on a ‘guillotine’
articles.summary: ABC argued in federal court Tuesday that President Donald Trump’s FCC has “chilled” the network’s free speech by using its “enormous regulatory power to coerce, threaten, punish” coverage the administration doesn’t like.
articles.body: ABC argued in federal court Tuesday that President Donald Trump’s FCC has “chilled” the network’s free speech by using its “enormous regulatory power to coerce, threaten, punish” coverage the administration doesn’t like. The Disney-owned network is seeking a preliminary injunction to block the FCC’s order requiring early renewal applications for all eight of the local stations it owns, even though those licenses don’t expire for years. ABC sued the government over the unusual order in August. The license-renewal order was an extraordinary escalation of the administration’s months-long effort to pressure ABC and Disney, which has included Trump’s repeated calls for ABC to fire Jimmy Kimmel and the FCC’s probes into Disney’s DEI practices, ABC’s relationship with its local affiliates, and whether “The View” violated the so-called “equal-time” rule. “We are chilled,” Beth Wilkinson, the attorney for ABC, told US District Judge Loren AliKhan during the nearly two-hour hearing. “We are watching everything that we do.” Wilkinson cited ABC’s decision not to carry Trump’s July prime-time address containing unverified election claims, saying that editorial choice had provoked “the anger in the administration and the retaliation from the agency.” During the address, Trump attacked ABC for not airing it and threatened the network’s station licenses. The threat of losing those station licenses, Wilkinson said, amounts to a “corporate death penalty” for ABC. Invoking the French Revolution, Wilkinson compared the administration’s pressure to keeping the network’s “head on the guillotine” as it continues reporting, leaving ABC to “wonder if anything we say is going to make that come down.” FCC lawyers argued that the US District Court lacks jurisdiction to review the agency’s license-renewal order and that ABC is a “regulated entity that is undergoing a review by its regulator” and cannot circumvent the regulatory process with this First Amendment case. Brendan Carr, the Trump-aligned FCC chair, has repeatedly asserted that the fight is all about Disney’s DEI practices, though former FCC officials from both parties have cast doubt on that claim. During an FCC meeting last week, Carr said Disney’s First Amendment lawsuit is a “very odd choice,” lodged “in the wrong court” and at “the wrong time.” Wilkinson took aim at Carr during the hearing, saying that Trump has “total control” over Carr and that the FCC chair “understands his marching orders.” The result, she said, has been “blatant violations of the US Constitution.” Judge AliKhan did not issue a ruling on Tuesday. She gave both sides through Wednesday, Oct. 14, to provide additional materials and responses.
